bank.q: The word meristem comes from the Greek meristos, which means...
bank.why: Meristos = divided. (Kolla = glue for collenchyma, skleros = hard, derma = skin.)

bank.q: Unspecialized cells that can divide indefinitely to produce new cells.
bank.why: Meristematic tissues are the plant's growth centers, like plant stem cells.

bank.q: Meristematic tissues are usually found at the...
bank.a: Apex (tips) of the root and shoot
bank.why: Meristems usually sit at the apices of roots and shoots.

bank.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of meristematic cells?
bank.a: They store large amounts of reserve food
d: They have dense protoplasm and conspicuous nuclei
Their vacuoles are few and small
bank.why: Meristematic cells do not store reserve food; they are in an active state of metabolism.

bank.q: Compared with mature cells, the vacuoles of meristematic cells are...
bank.why: Young dividing cells have not yet developed a large central vacuole.

bank.q: Meristematic cells are described in the slides as...
bank.why: They are compact shapes that fit together with little intercellular space.

bank.q: The early embryonic meristem from which other advanced meristems are derived.
bank.why: The promeristem is the earliest meristem; its function is to produce the primary meristems.

bank.q: The promeristem is composed of cells called...
bank.why: Promeristem is composed of initials, whose characteristic is continuous division.

bank.q: Derived from the promeristem and gives rise to the primary tissue systems.
bank.why: Primary meristems lie below the promeristem and divide to form permanent tissues.

bank.q: A secondary meristem is derived from...
bank.a: Permanent tissues that regain the capacity for division
bank.why: Secondary meristems come from mature or permanent cells that divide again (dedifferentiation).

bank.q: Which secondary meristem is responsible for the secondary thickening of plant organs?
bank.why: The vascular cambium makes secondary xylem (inside) and secondary phloem (outside).

bank.q: The cork cambium produces the...
bank.why: Cork cambium produces the periderm: cork outside, phelloderm inside.

bank.q: Located at the tips of roots and shoots; responsible for primary growth and increase in length.
bank.why: The apical meristem increases plant length.

bank.q: The intercalary meristem is present at the...
bank.a: Base of leaves, nodes and internodes
bank.why: Intercalary = inserted between; at leaf bases, nodes and internodes.

bank.q: This meristem lies on the side of the plant's body and gives the plant its width or girth.
bank.why: Lateral meristems (vascular and cork cambium) cause secondary growth.

bank.q: Which are lateral meristems?
bank.why: The vascular cambium and cork cambium are lateral meristems.

bank.q: Secondary growth refers to an increase in...
bank.why: Primary growth = length (apical); secondary growth = girth (lateral).

bank.q: The apical meristem produces which primary meristems?
bank.why: Apical meristem → protoderm, ground meristem and procambium → primary tissues.

bank.q: Which primary meristem develops into the epidermis?
bank.why: Protoderm → epidermis; ground meristem → ground tissue; procambium → primary xylem and phloem.

bank.q: Which primary meristem develops into the primary xylem and primary phloem?
bank.why: The procambium forms the primary vascular tissues.

bank.q: Which primary meristem gives rise to the cortex and pith?
bank.why: The ground meristem forms the ground tissue system (cortex and pith).

bank.q: Promeristem, primary and secondary meristems are classified according to their...
bank.why: By origin: promeristem, primary, secondary. By position: apical, intercalary, lateral.

bank.q: Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems are classified according to their...
bank.why: The second classification is based on position.

bank.q: A tree keeps growing taller every year, but its trunk does not increase in diameter. Which tissue is most likely not working?
bank.why: Height comes from the apical meristem; girth comes from the lateral meristem.

bank.q: A sapling's stem keeps getting thicker, but the plant no longer grows taller. What is most likely damaged?
bank.why: Increase in length is primary growth by the apical meristem at the shoot tip.

bank.q: Grass keeps growing back after it is mowed, even though the tips were cut off. Which meristem allows this?
bank.why: Intercalary meristems at leaf bases survive cutting or grazing and allow regrowth.

bank.q: A mutation in a seedling's shoot tip prevents a new outer covering from forming, but its vascular tissue and cortex develop normally. Which primary meristem is affected?
bank.why: Protoderm → epidermis. Procambium (vascular) and ground meristem (cortex) are working.

bank.q: New leaves form an epidermis and cortex but no new xylem or phloem. Which primary meristem is most likely affected?
bank.why: The procambium makes the primary xylem and phloem.

bank.q: An older woody stem keeps thickening, but its cracked outer covering is never replaced by new protective bark. What is most likely not functioning?
bank.why: The cork cambium produces the periderm that replaces the epidermis in older stems.

bank.q: A plant's root system spreads normally at the top, but the main root no longer grows deeper into the soil. Which tissue is most likely affected?
bank.why: The root apical meristem lengthens the root and pushes it deeper.

bank.q: A researcher wants to know whether the lengthening of bamboo internodes comes from the shoot tip or from the base of each internode. Which design is most appropriate?
bank.a: Mark the internodes with evenly spaced ink dots, remove the shoot tip from some plants but not others (control), and measure which spacing increases over time
d: Cut every internode at its base and see if the plant dies
Measure the total height of one plant once and compare it to a textbook value
Water half the plants more and count their leaves after a week
bank.why: Ink marks show where elongation happens, and keeping intact plants as a control isolates the role of the tip vs the intercalary meristem.
bank.hint: Mark, compare to a control, measure.

bank.q: Tissues made up of only one type of cell are called...
bank.why: Simple = one cell type; complex = two to several cell types.

bank.q: "Complex" in complex tissue refers to...
bank.a: Having two or more types of cells
bank.why: Simple and complex refer to the number of cell types, not difficulty.

bank.q: Which are the most abundant cell types in plants?
bank.why: Parenchyma cells are the most abundant and are found in all roots, stems, leaves and fruits.

bank.q: Which describes parenchyma cells?
bank.a: Living, thin primary wall, very large vacuoles
bank.why: Parenchyma: thin primary wall, very large vacuoles, living.

bank.q: Which is NOT a function of parenchyma?
bank.why: Rigid support is sclerenchyma's job; parenchyma photosynthesizes, stores and repairs.

bank.q: Parenchyma that contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis.
bank.why: Chloro = green; chlorenchyma has chloroplasts.

bank.q: Parenchyma that gives buoyancy to plants to help them float.
bank.why: Aerenchyma has large air spaces for buoyancy and oxygen movement.

bank.q: Collenchyma comes from the Greek kolla, meaning...
bank.why: Kolla = glue; the cells look closely joined.

bank.q: Compared with parenchyma, collenchyma cell walls are...
bank.why: Collenchyma has a thicker and more uneven wall than parenchyma, thickest at the corners.

bank.q: Collenchyma is usually found...
bank.a: Below the epidermis, in leaf blades and stalks
d: In the center of the root
In the vessels of the xylem
bank.why: Found in leaf blades and below the stalks, beneath the epidermis.

bank.q: The main function of collenchyma cells is to provide...
bank.why: Collenchyma supports young, growing parts while letting them bend.

bank.q: To provide support, both parenchyma and collenchyma cells must be...
bank.why: Support from these living cells depends on turgor pressure.

bank.q: Sclerenchyma comes from the Greek skleros, meaning...
bank.why: Skleros = hard.

bank.q: Sclerenchyma cells have a thick, tough secondary wall normally impregnated with...
bank.why: Lignin makes sclerenchyma walls hard and strong.

bank.q: At maturity, most sclerenchyma cells are...
bank.why: Most sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity; their walls remain as support.

bank.q: Sclerenchyma provides structural strength in regions that...
bank.a: Have stopped growing in length and no longer need to be flexible
bank.why: Collenchyma supports growing parts; sclerenchyma supports parts that stopped growing.

bank.q: Elongated sclerenchyma cells, usually in groups, that enable stems to move in the wind without snapping.
bank.why: Fibers are long and grouped; sclereids are short and make things rock-hard.

bank.q: Sclerenchyma cells, often cubical or spherical, that make structures rock-hard and inflexible.
bank.why: Sclereids (stone cells) harden nut shells, seed coats and the grit of pears.

bank.q: Which pair of simple tissues is alive at maturity?
bank.why: Parenchyma and collenchyma are living; sclerenchyma is mostly dead.

bank.q: The flexible strings of a celery stalk let it bend without breaking. Which tissue are they?
bank.why: Celery strings are collenchyma: living, unevenly thickened, flexible support.

bank.q: The gritty texture you feel when eating a pear comes from...
bank.why: Sclereids are very hard cells scattered in pear flesh.

bank.q: An aquatic plant's leaves photosynthesize normally, but they sink instead of floating. Which tissue is most likely defective?
bank.why: Aerenchyma's air spaces give buoyancy. Photosynthesis (chlorenchyma) is fine.

bank.q: A leaf's cells store water and heal wounds normally, but the leaf cannot make food. Which parenchyma type is most likely affected?
bank.why: Chlorenchyma is the photosynthetic parenchyma.

bank.q: A cut stem fails to form a callus over the wound, though the plant still photosynthesizes. Which cells normally regain the ability to divide and heal wounds?
bank.why: Parenchyma plays a vital role in wound healing and regeneration.

bank.q: A young herbaceous stem snaps easily in light wind, though it has plenty of water. Which tissue under its epidermis is most likely missing?
bank.why: Collenchyma gives young stems flexible support so they bend instead of snapping.

bank.q: A mature stem has stopped elongating but remains soft and weak, though its living cells are healthy. Which tissue is most likely lacking?
bank.why: Sclerenchyma gives rigid strength where growth has stopped.

bank.q: On a hot afternoon, a plant's young leaves and stems droop. Which explains why parenchyma and collenchyma stop supporting them?
bank.why: Both tissues must be turgid to provide support.

bank.term: Experiment: is it collenchyma or sclerenchyma?
bank.q: A student wants to know whether a stem's supporting cells are collenchyma or sclerenchyma. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Section the stem, stain it for lignin, and check under a microscope whether the cells are living with uneven walls or dead with thick lignified walls
d: Bend the whole plant until it breaks
Count the leaves on the stem
Leave the stem in the sun and see if it wilts
bank.why: Lignin staining and checking whether cells are alive separates collenchyma (living, unlignified) from sclerenchyma (dead, lignified).

bank.q: The three tissue systems of vascular plants are...
bank.why: Dermal, vascular and ground tissue systems, all from meristems.

bank.q: Complex tissues are organized into three tissue systems that are...
bank.why: They extend through roots, stems and leaves.

bank.q: Dermal comes from the Greek derma, meaning...
bank.why: Derma = skin; the dermal system is the outer covering.

bank.q: The outer protective covering of the plant that protects it from physical damage and desiccation.
bank.why: The dermal tissue is the outer protective covering.

bank.q: In a typical plant, the single layer of closely packed dermal cells forming a secure boundary is the...
bank.why: The epidermis is usually one layer of tightly packed cells.

bank.q: In plants with more than one growing season, the epidermis of the stem and root is replaced by the...
bank.why: The periderm (mainly cork) replaces the epidermis in older woody organs.

bank.q: The periderm consists mainly of...
bank.why: Cork cells protect plants from predators and water loss.

bank.q: Hair-like extensions of the dermal tissue that can inhibit herbivore attack.
bank.why: Trichomes defend by physical and/or chemical means.

bank.q: The stinging hairs of Urtica (nettle) deliver inflammatory chemicals such as...
bank.why: Specialized stinging trichomes of nettle deliver histamine.

bank.q: The thin waxy layer on top of the epidermis made of cutin, whose function is to prevent water loss.
bank.why: The cuticle is made of cutin and reduces water loss.

bank.q: The waxy cuticle is made of a fatty substance called...
bank.why: Cuticle = cutin; cork = suberin; hard walls = lignin.

bank.q: Highly specialized epidermal cells that contain chloroplasts and form the stomata.
bank.why: Guard cells form tiny pores (stomata) for gas exchange.

bank.q: The stomata allow...
bank.a: Gases to diffuse in and out of the leaves
d: Water to be pumped into the xylem
Food to be loaded into phloem
bank.why: Stomata are for gas exchange (and lose water vapor in transpiration).

bank.q: When guard cells absorb water and become turgid, the stoma usually...
bank.why: Turgid guard cells open the pore; when they lose water, it closes.

bank.q: The ground tissue system is also called the...
bank.why: Ground = fundamental tissue system.

bank.q: The ground tissue system consists of...
bank.a: All tissues other than the vascular and dermal tissue
bank.why: Ground tissue fills the plant between dermal and vascular tissues.

bank.q: Ground tissue found between the dermal and vascular tissue is called the...
bank.why: Cortex = between dermal and vascular; pith = inside the vascular tissue.

bank.q: Ground tissue that appears on the inside of the vascular tissues is called the...
bank.why: Pith is the central ground tissue.

bank.q: The ground tissue system is mostly made of...
bank.a: Parenchyma, with some collenchyma and sclerenchyma
bank.why: Ground tissue = mostly parenchyma plus collenchyma and sclerenchyma.

bank.q: A leaf's stomata and photosynthesis work normally, but it loses water rapidly through its surface even when the stomata are closed. What is most likely damaged?
bank.why: The cuticle prevents water loss through the surface; stomata are fine here.

bank.q: A leaf has a healthy cuticle and chlorenchyma, but carbon dioxide cannot enter it. Which cells are most likely not functioning?
bank.why: Gases enter through stomata formed by guard cells.

bank.q: A nettle plant grows normally but no longer irritates the skin of animals that brush against it. Which structure is most likely affected?
bank.why: Stinging trichomes deliver the irritating chemicals.

bank.q: An old tree trunk loses a lot of water and is easily attacked by insects, though its leaves are healthy. Which tissue is most likely failing?
bank.why: In older woody stems, the periderm protects from predators and water loss.

bank.q: Two varieties of a plant are equally green and healthy, but insects eat far more of variety A. Variety A most likely has fewer...
bank.why: Trichomes inhibit herbivore attack physically and chemically.

bank.term: Experiment: does the cuticle reduce water loss?
bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether the cuticle reduces water loss from leaves. What is the most appropriate design?
bank.a: Use leaves of the same plant and size, gently remove the wax from some leaves and leave others intact as controls, seal the stomata on all leaves, then weigh them at intervals under the same conditions
d: Remove the wax from one leaf and see if it looks dry the next day
Compare a leaf from a desert plant with a leaf from a water plant
Put all the leaves in water and count how many float
bank.why: Only the cuticle differs between the groups; sealed stomata and identical conditions remove other variables, and weighing measures the water lost.
bank.hint: Change only one thing; keep a control.

bank.q: Plants with a well-developed conductive system are called vascular plants or...
bank.why: Vascular plants are also called Tracheophyta.

bank.q: The main function of vascular tissue is...
bank.why: Main function: conduction of water, minerals and food; additional: mechanical support.

bank.q: Aside from conduction, vascular tissue also provides...
bank.why: Additional function: mechanical support.

bank.q: The name given to the contents transported by the xylem and phloem.
bank.why: Sap = contents of xylem and phloem.

bank.q: The main function of xylem is the conduction of...
bank.a: Water and minerals from the root to the rest of the plant
bank.why: Xylem: water and minerals upward. Phloem: food.

bank.q: The four xylem elements are...
bank.a: Tracheids, vessels, xylem fibers, xylem parenchyma
d: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibers, phloem parenchyma
Tracheids, sieve plates, sclereids, guard cells
bank.why: These four make xylem a complex tissue.

bank.q: Long cells with tapered ends; the fundamental cell type in xylem, non-living at maturity.
bank.why: Tracheids are long and tapered; water moves through pits.

bank.q: In tracheids, water moves from cell to cell through perforated portions of the wall called...
bank.why: Major portions of tracheid walls are perforated (pits).

bank.q: In the pit of a tracheid, which part acts as a valve?
bank.why: The torus seals the pit and stops air bubbles from spreading.

bank.q: Xylem vessels are also called...
bank.why: Vessels = trachea; their parts are vessel elements.

bank.q: Compared with tracheids, vessel elements are...
bank.why: Vessel elements are wider, shorter, less tapered tube-like cells.

bank.q: The openings in each vessel end wall are called...
bank.why: Vessel end walls have perforation plates; phloem end walls have sieve plates.

bank.q: Thread-like dead xylem cells whose main function is mechanical support.
bank.why: Xylem fibers support; they do not mainly conduct water.

bank.q: The only living cells of the xylem are the...
bank.why: Xylem parenchyma has cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus.

bank.q: Xylem parenchyma stores starch, oil and other...
bank.why: Ergastic substances are nonliving stored products like starch grains, oil, crystals.

bank.q: The main function of phloem is conduction of...
bank.a: Food and organic nutrients from the leaves to the rest of the plant
d: Water and minerals from the roots
bank.why: Phloem carries food (sugars) from sources to sinks.

bank.q: Primary phloem is derived from the...
bank.why: Primary phloem: procambium (primary growth). Secondary phloem: vascular cambium.

bank.q: Secondary phloem is derived from the...
bank.why: Secondary phloem forms from the vascular cambium.

bank.q: The phloem is composed of...
bank.a: Sieve-tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibers
bank.why: Four phloem elements.

bank.q: Living phloem cells with protoplasm but no lignified wall, which lack a nucleus at maturity.
bank.why: Sieve-tube elements are alive but lose their nucleus.

bank.q: Pores in the end walls that let materials pass from one sieve-tube element to the next.
bank.why: Sieve plates are the porous end walls of sieve-tube elements.

bank.q: Specialized parenchyma cells that keep their nucleus and supply proteins to the sieve-tube members.
bank.why: Companion cells have a nucleus and support the sieve tube.

bank.q: Companion cells are connected to sieve tubes by...
bank.why: Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels through the cell walls.

bank.q: Thin-walled living phloem cells that primarily help store starch.
bank.why: Phloem parenchyma stores starch.

bank.q: Long phloem cells that provide support for the plant (bast fibers).
bank.why: Phloem fibers provide support.

bank.q: Which xylem conducting cells are dead at maturity?
bank.why: Water-conducting cells are dead, hollow tubes; phloem conducting cells are alive.

bank.q: A plant's roots absorb water normally from wet soil, but its leaves wilt. Food transport is normal. What is most likely blocked?
bank.why: Xylem carries water from the roots to the leaves.

bank.q: A plant's leaves photosynthesize normally and stay green, but its roots stop growing because they receive no sugar. Which tissue is most likely blocked?
bank.why: Phloem moves food from the leaves to the roots.

bank.q: The sieve-tube elements in a plant are intact but quickly stop working because they receive no proteins. Which cells are most likely defective?
bank.why: Sieve-tube elements have no nucleus; companion cells supply their proteins.

bank.q: A plant's xylem still conducts water, but it can no longer store starch in that tissue. Which xylem cell is most likely affected?
bank.why: Xylem parenchyma, the only living xylem cells, store starch and oil.

bank.q: A stem conducts water and food normally, but its vascular bundles collapse under their own weight. Which cells are most likely lacking?
bank.why: Xylem fibers' main function is mechanical support.

bank.q: In a conifer, an air bubble in one tracheid spreads to all its neighbors instead of being sealed off. Which part of the pit is most likely not working?
bank.why: The torus acts as a valve that seals the pit.

bank.q: Plant A conducts water much faster than Plant B. Plant A most likely has more...
bank.why: Vessels are wider and have open end walls, so they conduct water faster.

bank.q: A researcher wants to show that phloem, not xylem, carries sugar down from the leaves. What is the most appropriate method?
bank.a: Remove a ring of bark (phloem) from some stems while leaving others intact as controls, then compare sugar build-up above the ring and the health of the roots over time
d: Cut off all the leaves and measure the height of the plant
Put dye in the soil and check whether the flowers change color
Water half the plants with sugar water
bank.why: Ringing removes only the phloem (outside the wood), so sugar accumulates above the ring and roots starve, while the xylem keeps moving water.
bank.hint: Remove only one tissue, keep controls.

bank.q: A student wants to see which tissue carries water up a celery stalk. Which approach is best?
bank.a: Stand a freshly cut stalk in colored water, keep another in plain water as a control, then cut cross-sections after some hours and see which tissue is stained
d: Leave the celery in the dark for a week
Weigh the celery before and after cooking
Peel the celery and count its strings
bank.why: The dye moves with the water through the xylem, which shows up as stained dots in the cross-section.

bank.q: Which part forms the descending portion of the plant?
bank.why: The root forms the descending portion; the stem the ascending axis.

bank.q: Roots are typically...
bank.why: Roots are non-green and brownish.

bank.q: Which structures are absent in a typical root?
bank.why: Roots lack nodes, internodes, leaves and buds; stems have them.

bank.q: The root tip is covered by a root cap called the...
bank.why: Root cap = calyptra.

bank.q: Roots are...
bank.a: Positively hydrotropic, negatively phototropic, positively geotropic
d: Negatively hydrotropic, positively phototropic, negatively geotropic
bank.why: Roots grow toward water and gravity and away from light.

bank.q: Roots growing downward, in the direction of gravity, show...
bank.why: Geotropism = gravitropism; roots are positive, shoots negative.

bank.q: In roots, the vascular bundles are...
bank.why: Root vascular bundles are radial; xylem is exarch.

bank.q: Unicellular structures near the root tip for water absorption.
bank.why: Root hairs are single epidermal-cell extensions that increase surface area.

bank.q: The two types of root systems are...
bank.a: Tap root and adventitious root systems
bank.why: Tap root and adventitious root systems.

bank.q: The tap root system originates from the...
bank.why: The tap root develops from the radicle (embryonic root).

bank.q: A single deep-seated main root, thick at the base and tapering toward the apex, with secondary and tertiary roots.
bank.why: That is the tap root system.

bank.q: Many roots of equal length that act as surface feeders.
bank.why: Adventitious roots are many, of equal size, and feed near the surface.

bank.q: Adventitious roots arise from the...
bank.why: Adventitious roots arise from any part other than the radicle.

bank.q: The tap root system is common in...
bank.why: Tap root: dicots. Adventitious: monocots.

bank.q: The adventitious root system is common in...
bank.why: Adventitious (fibrous) roots are common in monocots like grasses and corn.

bank.q: Roots have no bud-derived branches like stems, but lateral roots arise internally from the...
bank.why: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle, an internal tissue.

bank.q: A seedling's roots grow sideways and toward a lamp instead of down, though they still absorb water. Which normal root responses have failed?
bank.why: Roots should grow with gravity and away from light.

bank.q: During a long drought, a mango tree survives while nearby grasses dry out. Which root system feature explains this?
bank.a: Its tap root reaches deep water
d: Its adventitious roots feed at the surface
bank.why: Tap roots go deep; adventitious roots are surface feeders.

bank.q: Which root system is better at holding the topsoil in place on a slope?
bank.why: Many equal surface roots form a dense mat that holds topsoil.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether roots respond more to water or to gravity. What are the most appropriate steps?
bank.a: Grow seedlings in the dark to remove light, first test gravity alone by rotating some on a clinostat (to cancel gravity) against unrotated controls, then test water alone by placing a damp cloth on one side while keeping gravity constant, and compare root bending
d: Plant seeds in wet soil under sunlight and see which way the roots grow
Water the seedlings from above and measure how tall they grow
Put the seedlings next to a window with a damp cloth on top and observe for a day
bank.why: Each stimulus is tested alone: light removed, gravity canceled by rotation vs controls, then moisture on one side with gravity held constant.
bank.hint: Isolate one stimulus at a time.

bank.q: A student wants to show that roots are negatively phototropic. Which is the best setup?
bank.a: Grow seedlings in transparent containers with light from one side only, keep identical seedlings in total darkness as controls, keep water and gravity the same for both, and compare the direction of root growth
d: Grow seedlings under a lamp from above and count the roots
Grow seedlings in the dark only
Expose half the seedlings to light and give them more water
bank.why: Light from one side is the only difference from the dark controls, so any bending away from it shows phototropism.

bank.q: Which is the correct order of the parts of a typical root from the tip upward?
bank.a: Root cap, meristematic zone, zone of elongation, root hair zone, zone of maturation
d: Root hair zone, root cap, elongation, meristematic, maturation
Meristematic zone, root cap, maturation, elongation, root hair zone
Root cap, elongation, meristematic, maturation, root hair zone
bank.why: Tip upward: cap → division → elongation → root hairs → maturation.

bank.q: The root cap is cap-like, multicellular and...
bank.why: Root cap: cap-like, at the apex, multicellular, parenchymatous.

bank.q: The root cap protects the growing point against...
bank.why: It shields the meristem as the root pushes through soil.

bank.q: The root cap is rich in starch, which helps in...
bank.why: Starch grains (amyloplasts) settle with gravity so the root knows which way is down.

bank.q: The root cap is rich in Golgi bodies because its outer cells secrete...
bank.a: Mucilage that lubricates the root tip
bank.why: Golgi bodies help make mucilage, which lubricates the tip.

bank.q: In hydrophytes like Eichhornia, Pistia and Lemna, the root cap is replaced by...
bank.a: Root pockets that help in balancing
bank.why: Water plants have root pockets instead of a typical root cap.

bank.q: Multiple root caps are found in the stilt roots of...
bank.why: Pandanus stilt roots have multiple root caps.

bank.q: In mycorrhizal roots, the root cap may be...
bank.why: Mycorrhizal roots may have reduced or absent root caps.

bank.q: The growing point (meristematic zone) of the root is about how long?
bank.why: Root apex about 1 mm; zone of elongation 4–8 mm.

bank.q: The zone of cell division in a root is the...
bank.why: Cells actively divide in the meristematic zone.

bank.q: In the meristematic zone, cells toward the apex develop into the...
bank.why: Toward the apex → calyptrogen (makes the cap); toward the base → histogen.

bank.q: In the meristematic zone, cells toward the base form the...
bank.why: Toward the base, the cells form the histogen (root tissues).

bank.q: 4–8 mm long; cells elongate due to vacuolization and lose the power of cell division.
bank.why: Cells lengthen as their vacuoles enlarge.

bank.q: In the zone of elongation, cells lengthen because of...
bank.why: Vacuoles enlarge and merge, stretching the cells.

bank.q: The root hair zone is also called the...
bank.why: Pili = hairs; piliferous region = root hair zone.

bank.q: Root hairs are...
bank.why: Root hairs are single cells and short-lived.

bank.q: Which region is the principal site of water and mineral absorption?
bank.why: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area for absorption.

bank.q: Which zone is described as temporary and moves forward with the growth of the root tip?
bank.why: New hairs form near the tip as older ones die.

bank.q: Above the root hair zone; forms the bulk; cells thick-walled with no water absorption; lateral roots arise here.
bank.why: The zone of maturation forms the bulk; secondary growth occurs here.

bank.q: Lateral roots and secondary growth arise in the...
bank.why: Lateral roots arise from the zone of maturation.

bank.q: A root grows in random directions though it absorbs water normally. Which structure most likely lost its starch-filled cells?
bank.why: Starch in the root cap helps sense gravity.

bank.q: A root's tip is repeatedly torn as it pushes through soil, though cells behind it divide normally. Which structure is most likely missing?
bank.why: The root cap protects the growing point from soil friction.

bank.q: A root's cells divide normally at the tip, but the root does not push deeper because the new cells stay short. Which zone is affected?
bank.why: In the zone of elongation, cells lengthen by vacuolization and push the tip down.

bank.q: A root stops producing new cells altogether, so all zones behind it gradually disappear. Which zone is most likely damaged?
bank.why: The meristematic zone is the zone of cell division.

bank.q: A plant's roots are long and well anchored, but water absorption is very poor. Which zone is most likely damaged?
bank.why: The root hair zone is the main absorption region.

bank.q: A root absorbs water and grows longer normally but never forms lateral roots. Which zone is most likely affected?
bank.why: Lateral roots arise from the zone of maturation.

bank.q: A root tip becomes dry and rough and drags against soil particles, though its cap cells are present. What is most likely missing?
bank.why: Outer root-cap cells secrete mucilage that lubricates the tip.

bank.term: Experiment: where does the root grow?
bank.q: A researcher wants to find which root zone is responsible for most of the increase in length. What is the best method?
bank.a: Mark a young root with evenly spaced ink lines from the tip, grow it in moist air beside an unmarked control, and measure which spaces widen after 24 hours
d: Cut off the root tip and see if the plant survives
Measure the length of a mature root once
Grow the plant in sand and count its root hairs
bank.why: The spaces that widen most show where cells elongate; a control root confirms the ink does not affect growth.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for food storage?
bank.why: Root function examples: food storage = Carrot and radish.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for extra mechanical support?
bank.why: Root function examples: extra mechanical support = Banyan and maize.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for aeration?
bank.why: Root function examples: aeration = Mangroves.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for reproduction?
bank.why: Root function examples: reproduction = Dahlia.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for floating?
bank.why: Root function examples: floating = Jussiaea.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for photosynthesis?
bank.why: Root function examples: photosynthesis = Tinospora.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for nitrogen fixation?
bank.why: Root function examples: nitrogen fixation = Pea.

bank.term: Absorbing food from a host: example
bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for absorbing food from a host?
bank.why: Root function examples: absorbing food from a host = Cuscuta.

bank.term: Absorbing water from the air: example
bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for absorbing water from the air?
bank.why: Root function examples: absorbing water from the air = Vanda.

bank.q: In the slides, which plant is the example of roots used for climbing?
bank.why: Root function examples: climbing = Pothos.

bank.q: Mycorrhizal roots are specialized for the absorption of...
bank.why: Mycorrhizal roots help absorb phosphates.

bank.q: Which plant has green roots, per the slides?
bank.why: Green roots: Trapa (water chestnut).

bank.q: In tap roots modified for storage, which is true?
bank.a: The tap root is swollen and fleshy while secondary roots remain thin
d: The stem becomes long and woody
The root becomes green and photosynthetic
bank.why: The tap root stores food; secondary roots stay thin; the stem is reduced and disc-like with radical leaves.

bank.q: The reserve food of storage tap roots is utilized at the time of...
d: Germination of the next generation only
bank.why: Reserve food is used at flowering and fruiting.

bank.q: Cone-shaped; swollen at the base and gradually tapering toward the apex. This tap root modification is...
bank.why: Conical = cone-shaped; swollen at the base and gradually tapering toward the apex. Example: Carrot.

bank.q: Which is an example of a conical tap root?
bank.why: Conical: Carrot.

bank.q: Spindle-shaped; thick in the middle and tapering at the base and apex. This tap root modification is...
bank.why: Fusiform = spindle-shaped; thick in the middle and tapering at the base and apex. Example: Radish.

bank.q: Which is an example of a fusiform tap root?
bank.why: Fusiform: Radish.

bank.q: Swollen at the base, almost spherical, and suddenly thin toward the apex. This tap root modification is...
bank.why: Napiform = swollen at the base, almost spherical, and suddenly thin toward the apex. Example: Turnip.

bank.q: Which is an example of a napiform tap root?
bank.why: Napiform: Turnip.

bank.q: A tap root that becomes swollen with no definite shape, as in Mirabilis.
bank.why: Tuberous tap root: no definite shape (Mirabilis).

bank.q: In a fusiform root (radish), about two-thirds of the fleshy part is formed by the...
bank.why: Hypocotyl forms 2/3 of the fleshy part; the terminal part is the tap root.

bank.q: Fleshy with no definite shape, arising singly at each node, storing starch. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Tuberous (adventitious): fleshy with no definite shape, arising singly at each node, storing starch.

bank.q: Swollen roots in clusters from the lower nodes of the stem. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Fasciculated: swollen roots in clusters from the lower nodes of the stem.

bank.q: Beaded roots. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Moniliform: beaded roots.

bank.q: Roots whose apical portions are swollen. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Nodulose: roots whose apical portions are swollen.

bank.q: Roots with swellings as a series of ring-like outgrowths. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Annulated: roots with swellings as a series of ring-like outgrowths.

bank.q: Roots like the palm of a human hand. This adventitious root modification is...
bank.why: Palmate: roots like the palm of a human hand.

bank.q: Dahlia's fasciculated roots store food in the form of...
bank.why: Dahlia stores inulin; sweet potato stores starch.

bank.q: Adventitious roots arising from the lower nodes of the stem, as in sugarcane.
bank.why: Stilt roots arise from the lower nodes and give extra support.

bank.q: Mangroves are halophytes growing in coastal salt-water wetlands. What problem does their habitat pose?
bank.a: Excess salt and water make anchoring, aeration and seed germination difficult
bank.why: Salty waterlogged mud is low in oxygen and soft.

bank.q: Respiratory roots of mangroves growing in oxygen-deficient areas.
bank.why: Pneuma = air; pneumatophores are breathing roots.

bank.q: Pneumatophores produce aerial branches that are...
bank.why: They grow up out of the mud to reach air.

bank.q: Near their tips, pneumatophores bear ___ for exchange of gases.
bank.why: Pneumatophores bear lenticels near the tip.

bank.q: Which are examples of plants with pneumatophores?
bank.why: Avicennia and Sonneratia have pneumatophores; Rhizophora has stilt roots.

bank.q: By nature, pneumatophores are modified...
bank.why: Nature: modified secondary roots; function: gaseous exchange.

bank.q: Rhizophora has which supporting roots?
bank.why: Supporting roots: stilt roots in Rhizophora.

bank.q: In mangroves, seeds germinating while still attached to the parent plant is called...
bank.why: Vivipary helps seedlings survive waterlogged conditions.

bank.q: Which statement is correct?
bank.a: Sweet potato is a modified root; potato is a modified stem
d: Sweet potato is a stem; potato is a root
bank.why: Sweet potato (tuberous adventitious root) has no eyes; potato is a stem tuber with eyes.

bank.q: Mangrove seedlings in a mud flat have normal leaves and stilt roots, but their roots die from lack of oxygen. Which structures are most likely missing?
bank.why: Pneumatophores bring air to roots in oxygen-poor mud.

bank.q: Corn plants with healthy leaves keep falling over in strong wind. Which roots most likely failed to develop?
bank.why: Stilt roots from the lower nodes give extra mechanical support.

bank.q: A pea plant grows well only when given nitrogen fertilizer, unlike its neighbors. What is most likely missing from its roots?
bank.why: Pea roots fix nitrogen through nodules (Rhizobium).

bank.q: An epiphytic Vanda orchid hanging in humid air begins to dry out though its roots are intact. Which root function is most likely impaired?
bank.why: Vanda's aerial roots absorb water from the air.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether pneumatophores supply oxygen to mangrove roots. What is the best design?
bank.a: Cover the pneumatophores of some trees with a waterproof coating, leave others uncovered as controls in the same mud flat, and compare oxygen levels and health of the underground roots over time
d: Cut down one mangrove and look at its roots
Count how many pneumatophores grow per square meter
Move a mangrove to dry soil and see if it survives
bank.why: Blocking only the pneumatophores' lenticels, with controls in the same habitat, isolates their role in aeration.
bank.hint: Block only one structure; compare with controls.

bank.q: The area of soil where the plant exudes vitamins, hormones and other substances that promote the growth of microbes.
bank.why: Rhizosphere = soil around the root.

bank.q: A microhabitat formed by the association of microbes with the root surface.
bank.why: Rhizoplane = the root surface itself.

bank.q: Bacteria in the rhizosphere that promote plant growth are called...
bank.why: PGPR (slide: PGRR) = plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the four root–microbe interactions listed?
bank.why: The four: mycorrhiza, reciprocal symbiosis in nodules, associative symbiosis, mycotrophy.

bank.q: A symbiotic association of a saprophytic fungus with the roots of higher plants.
bank.why: Myco = fungus, rhiza = root.

bank.q: In mycorrhizal roots like those of Pinus, root hairs are replaced by...
bank.why: The hyphae act as root hairs; roots are shallow with no cap or hairs.

bank.q: The bulk of the fungus lives outside the root, forming a thick woolly sheath.
bank.why: Ecto = outside; Pinus, Eucalyptus, oak.

bank.q: Ectotrophic mycorrhiza is found in...
bank.why: Ectotrophic: Pinus, Eucalyptus, oak. Endotrophic: orchids, crops, grasses.

bank.q: The bulk of the fungus occurs inside the root's cortex cells, forming vesicles and arbuscules.
bank.why: Endo = inside the cells.

bank.q: In endomycorrhiza, the vesicles formed inside the cortex cells store...
bank.why: Vesicles store lipids; arbuscules transfer nutrients.

bank.q: In endomycorrhiza, the finger-like structures that transfer nutrients from fungus to root are...
bank.why: Arbuscules = tree-like exchange structures.

bank.q: The common type of endomycorrhiza that helps in phosphate absorption is...
bank.why: VAM helps in phosphate absorption.

bank.q: The fungal partner in endotrophic mycorrhiza belongs to the...
bank.why: Per the slide: zygomycetes, such as Armillaria.

bank.q: A pine seedling grown in sterilized soil develops poorly and shows phosphate deficiency, while seedlings in forest soil are healthy. What is most likely missing?
bank.why: Mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphate and water uptake; sterilized soil lacks them.

bank.q: Under a microscope, a root is wrapped in a thick woolly layer of fungus, but the fungus does not enter the cells. This is...
bank.why: Ectotrophic: the fungus is outside, forming a sheath.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether soil microbes promote a crop's growth. What is the best design?
bank.a: Grow identical seedlings in the same soil, sterilizing half of it and leaving half unsterilized, with the same light, water and nutrients, then compare growth and root colonization
d: Grow one plant in forest soil and one in a pot and compare their heights
Add fertilizer to all plants and measure their leaves
Use different crop species in each soil
bank.why: Only the presence of live microbes differs between the groups.

bank.q: The plant axis that bears buds and shoots with leaves and, at its basal end, roots.
bank.why: The stem is the central axis of the plant.

bank.q: The plant stem has been described as the...
bank.a: Central axis to which all other parts are attached
bank.why: The stem is the central axis; roots are the descending portion.

bank.q: The first stem that develops from a seed arises from the...
bank.why: The epicotyl is the embryonic shoot within the seed.

bank.q: The shoot system, including the stem, shows which response?
bank.why: Stems are phototropic; roots are negatively phototropic.

bank.q: Lateral branches of the stem arise in the...
bank.why: Lateral branches arise in the angle between leaf and stem.

bank.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of a stem?
d: Bears nodes, internodes, leaves and flowers
bank.why: Stems have nodes and internodes; roots lack them.

bank.q: A stem's primary growing point.
bank.why: Buds are leaf (vegetative) or flower (reproductive) buds.

bank.q: Buds that are vegetative develop into...
bank.why: Leaf buds are vegetative; flower buds are reproductive.

bank.q: The terminal bud releases the hormone...
bank.why: Auxin from the terminal bud suppresses lateral buds.

bank.q: Auxin from the terminal bud suppresses the lateral buds, focusing growth...
bank.why: This is apical dominance.

bank.q: Buds that grow from the leaf axils on the side of a stem.
bank.why: Lateral buds sit in the leaf axils.

bank.q: A modified leaf protecting and covering a bud.
bank.why: Bud scales protect dormant buds.

bank.q: When a leaf falls, the mark it leaves on the stem is the...
bank.why: Leaf scar = whole mark; bundle scars are inside it.

bank.q: A mark left in the leaf scar from the vascular tissue attachment, used in identifying woody plants.
bank.why: Bundle scars are inside the leaf scar.

bank.q: Pores in the stem that allow for gas exchange.
bank.why: Lenticels are pores in bark for gas exchange.

bank.q: The segment of the stem where leaves and lateral buds are attached.
bank.why: Nodes bear leaves and buds.

bank.q: The section of a stem between two nodes.
bank.why: Inter = between.

bank.q: The protective outer tissue of woody plants that develops with age.
bank.why: Bark protects woody stems and develops with age.

bank.q: Stems with no permanent woody tissue, a short lifespan, and dying soon after flowering, as in banana.
bank.why: Herbaceous: soft, short-lived (banana).

bank.q: Stems that are more or less woody or half-woody, usually at the basal part, as in eggplant and jute.
bank.why: Suffrutescent = half-woody at the base.

bank.q: Stems of shrubs and trees that form permanent woody tissue made of secondary xylem.
bank.why: The woody part is secondary xylem.

bank.q: The woody portion of a woody stem is made of...
bank.why: Wood = secondary xylem made by the vascular cambium.

bank.q: Banana is given in the slides as an example of which stem texture?
bank.why: Banana: herbaceous; eggplant and jute: suffrutescent; trees: woody.

bank.q: A gardener cuts off the tip of a plant's main stem. Two weeks later, many side branches appear. What explains this?
bank.a: Removing the terminal bud removed the auxin that suppressed the lateral buds
d: Cutting increased the auxin in the lateral buds
The bark grew faster after injury
bank.why: Apical dominance is lost when the terminal bud is removed.

bank.q: A plant grows very tall with almost no side branches, even though its axillary buds are healthy. What is most likely responsible?
bank.a: Strong auxin from the terminal bud (apical dominance)
bank.why: Auxin from the terminal bud keeps the lateral buds suppressed.

bank.q: A woody stem has a healthy bark that protects it, but its inner living tissues lack oxygen. Which structures are most likely blocked?
bank.why: Lenticels are the stem's pores for gas exchange.

bank.q: In a cold winter, a tree's dormant buds dry out and die, though its trunk is healthy. Which structure most likely failed?
bank.why: Bud scales are modified leaves that protect buds.

bank.q: In winter, a botanist must identify a leafless woody plant. Which feature on the twig is specifically mentioned in the slides as useful?
bank.why: Bundle scars are used in the identification of woody plants.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether the terminal bud's auxin suppresses lateral buds. Which design is most appropriate?
bank.a: Use three groups of identical plants: intact (control), terminal bud removed, and terminal bud removed with auxin paste applied to the cut; then count lateral branches after some weeks
d: Remove the terminal bud from one plant and look at it the next day
Spray auxin on the leaves of all plants and measure their height
Compare a tall tree with a short shrub
bank.why: Replacing the bud with auxin paste shows that auxin, not just the bud, controls the lateral buds; the intact plants are the control.
bank.hint: Remove it, then add the hormone back.

bank.q: Modified stems are grouped under three heads:
bank.why: Modified stems: underground, subaerial, aerial.

bank.q: Which is NOT a function of underground stems?
bank.why: Underground stems protect, store food, and propagate.

bank.q: An underground stem can be distinguished from a root by the presence of...
bank.a: Nodes, internodes, scale leaves, axillary buds and a terminal bud
d: A root cap and root hairs
bank.why: Stem features prove stem nature even underground.

bank.q: The four types of underground stems are...
bank.why: Underground: rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm.

bank.q: A thick, horizontally growing underground stem that usually stores food material.
bank.why: Rhizome: horizontal, with nodes, scale leaves, buds, adventitious roots.

bank.q: Which are examples of rhizomes?
bank.why: Rhizome: ginger, turmeric.

bank.q: In a rhizome, roots develop from the...
bank.why: Roots develop from the lower surface.

bank.q: A swollen end of an underground branch that arises from the axil of a lower leaf.
bank.why: The tuber is the swollen tip of an underground branch.

bank.q: A leaf scar with an axillary bud on a potato is called a/an...
bank.why: Leaf scar + axillary bud = eye.

bank.q: A tuber is irregular in shape due to the deposition of...
bank.why: Food (starch) deposition makes it irregular.

bank.q: Which is the example of a stem tuber in the slides?
bank.why: Potato is a stem tuber; sweet potato is a root.

bank.q: The stem is reduced to a short disc and its lower surface produces many adventitious roots.
bank.why: Bulb: disc-like stem, fleshy leaves (onion, garlic).

bank.q: In onion, the inner leaves are fleshy while the outer ones are dry, and the concentric leaf bases form a complete covering. This is a...
bank.why: Tunic = complete covering.

bank.q: In garlic, daughter bulbs (cloves) are produced by the...
bank.why: The axillary buds sometimes produce daughter bulbs.

bank.q: In a bulb, food is stored mainly in the...
bank.why: Bulbs store food in fleshy leaf bases; corms store food in the stem.

bank.q: Which part of a bulb produces the main shoot?
bank.why: The apical bud of the bulb produces the shoot.

bank.q: A greatly swollen underground basal portion of an erect stem, swollen due to stored food.
bank.why: Corm: solid swollen stem base (Colocasia).

bank.q: Which are examples of corms?
bank.why: Corm: Amorphophallus, Colocasia (gabi/taro).

bank.q: At the end of the growing season, what happens to a corm?
bank.a: The aerial parts die; later a bud uses the stored food, a new corm forms, and the old one shrivels
d: The corm turns into a bulb
The corm grows horizontally into a rhizome
bank.why: One bud uses the reserves; the new plant forms a new corm; the old shrivels.

bank.q: A bulb stores food mainly in its ___, while a corm stores food in its ___.
bank.why: Bulb = leaves; corm = stem.

bank.q: A farmer plants potato pieces, but one piece never sprouts though it is full of starch. What does that piece most likely lack?
bank.why: New plants grow from the eyes; a piece without an eye cannot sprout.

bank.term: Is it a stem or root?
bank.q: A student finds a swollen underground organ with nodes, scale leaves and buds. What should they conclude?
d: It is a modified leaf only
bank.why: Nodes, internodes, scale leaves and buds prove stem nature.

bank.q: An onion bulb's fleshy leaves rot and dry quickly in storage. Which part normally protects them?
bank.why: The dry outer leaves form a protective tunic.

bank.q: A ginger plant grows aerial shoots but never spreads to new ground underground. Which part of the rhizome is most likely damaged?
bank.a: Terminal bud (growing point) of the rhizome
bank.why: The rhizome's growing point stays underground and elongates it horizontally.

bank.term: Experiment: is the potato a stem?
bank.q: A student wants to show that a potato is a stem and not a root. Which approach is best?
bank.a: Cut potato pieces with an eye and without an eye, plant them under identical conditions, and record which sprout shoots; also look for nodes and scale-leaf scars
d: Boil the potato and taste it
Measure the weight of the potato
Peel the potato and count the starch grains
bank.why: Only pieces with eyes (buds at nodes) sprout, which shows stem features roots lack.

bank.q: Subaerial stems are modified mainly for...
bank.why: Runners, offsets, stolons and suckers spread the plant without seeds.

bank.q: A lateral branch from the base of the stem that runs along the surface of the soil, producing roots below and leaves above at each node.
bank.why: Runner: along the soil surface (Oxalis, strawberry, Centella).

bank.q: Which are examples of runners?
bank.why: Runners: Oxalis, Fragaria, Centella asiatica.

bank.q: A short, thick, runner-like branch that produces a new plant at its tip and grows in all directions.
bank.why: Offset: Pistia, Eichhornia.

bank.q: Which are examples of offsets?
bank.why: Offsets: water lettuce (Pistia) and water hyacinth (Eichhornia).

bank.q: A lateral branch from the underground stem that grows horizontally in the soil, then its terminal bud emerges and forms a new plant.
bank.why: Stolon example: Colocasia.
bank.hint: Grows in the soil, emerges at the tip.

bank.q: Which is the slides' example of a stolon?
bank.why: Stolon: Colocasia.

bank.q: A lateral branch near ground level that travels underground for some distance, turns up at its end, and produces a new plant.
bank.why: Sucker example: Chrysanthemum.

bank.q: Which is the slides' example of a sucker?
bank.why: Sucker: Chrysanthemum.

bank.q: Coiling stem modifications that help plants climb; the terminal bud forms one in Cissus quadrangularis.
bank.why: Stem tendrils come from the terminal bud (Cissus) or axillary bud (passion fruit).

bank.q: In passion fruit, the tendril develops from the...
bank.why: Cissus: terminal bud; passion fruit: axillary bud.

bank.q: A hard, straight, pointed structure that may bear leaves, flowers and fruits, as in Duranta and pomegranate.
bank.why: Thorns are modified stems and can bear leaves, flowers and fruits.

bank.q: Stem thorns...
bank.a: Check transpiration and protect the plant from grazing
bank.why: Thorns check transpiration and protect from herbivores.

bank.q: Which is correct?
bank.a: Thorns are modified stems, spines are modified leaves, prickles lack vascular tissue
d: Thorns are modified leaves, spines are modified stems
Prickles are modified stems with vascular tissue
bank.why: Thorn = stem, spine = leaf, prickle = surface outgrowth without vascular tissue.

bank.q: A flattened stem of several internodes functioning as a leaf.
bank.why: Phylloclade example: Opuntia.

bank.q: In Opuntia, the clusters of spines on the phylloclade are modified...
bank.why: These spines are the modified leaves of the axillary bud.

bank.q: A phylloclade of one or two internodes is called a...
bank.why: Cladode = phylloclade of 1–2 internodes.

bank.q: A flattened leaf-like stem arising in the axil of a minute, bract-like true leaf, as in Asparagus.
bank.why: Asparagus has cladophylls (also called cladodes).

bank.q: A special multicellular body essentially meant for reproduction, as in Agave and Dioscorea.
bank.why: Bulbils detach and grow into new plants.

bank.q: In Agave, bulbils are modified from...
bank.why: Agave: floral buds → bulbils. Dioscorea: axillary bud → bulbil.

bank.q: In Dioscorea, the bulbil develops from the...
bank.why: Dioscorea: axillary bud becomes a bulbil.

bank.q: A strawberry plant flowers and fruits normally but never forms new plants around it. Which structure is most likely not forming?
bank.why: Strawberry spreads by runners.

bank.q: A Cissus quadrangularis vine grows long but cannot attach to its trellis, though its leaves are healthy. Which structure is most likely affected?
bank.why: Cissus climbs with stem tendrils from the terminal bud.

bank.q: An Opuntia plant's spines are normal, but its flat green pads cannot photosynthesize. Which structure is affected?
bank.why: In Opuntia, the flattened stem (phylloclade) does the photosynthesis.

bank.q: Water hyacinth quickly covers a pond by forming daughter plants in all directions. Which modification explains this?
bank.why: Eichhornia reproduces by offsets.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether strawberry daughter plants depend on the runner for water. What is the best design?
bank.a: Use plants with rooted daughter plants, cut the runner in some and leave it intact in others, water only the mother plants, and compare the daughters' survival
d: Cut all the runners and observe one plant
Water all plants heavily and count their fruits
Grow the plants without daughter plants
bank.why: Watering only the mothers makes the runner the only possible water source; cut vs intact runners isolate its role.
bank.hint: Make the runner the only variable.

bank.q: The thin, flat lateral outgrowths from stem nodes.
bank.why: Leaves are lateral outgrowths of nodes.

bank.q: Leaves are the main vegetative organs concerned with...
bank.why: Main leaf functions.

bank.q: Leaves are produced from a superficial meristematic tissue called...
bank.why: Leaves come from leaf primordia, so they are exogenous.

bank.q: Because leaves arise from superficial tissue, they are described as...
bank.why: Exogenous = from outer tissues (lateral roots are endogenous, from the pericycle).

bank.q: The same plant bearing different kinds of leaves.
bank.why: Hetero = different, phyll = leaf.

bank.q: In Limnophila heterophylla, the submerged part bears ___ leaves and the aerial part bears ___ leaves.
bank.why: Underwater leaves are dissected; aerial leaves are entire.

bank.term: Three parts of a dicot leaf
bank.q: A typical dicot leaf has which three parts?
bank.a: Leaf base, leaf stalk, leaf lamina
bank.why: Base (hypopodium), stalk (mesopodium), lamina (epipodium).

bank.q: The leaf base is also called the...
bank.why: Hypo = below.

bank.q: The leaf stalk is also called the...
bank.why: Meso = middle.

bank.q: The leaf lamina is also called the...
bank.why: Epi = upon/top.

bank.q: The upper angle between the leaf base and the stem.
bank.why: Axillary buds sit in the axil.

bank.q: A swollen leaf base, as in Leguminosae.
bank.why: Leaves with a pulvinus are pulvinate (Mimosa pudica, mango).

bank.q: In Mimosa, which structure is responsible for the sleep movement of leaves (nyctinasty)?
bank.why: Turgor changes in the pulvinus move the leaf.

bank.q: In monocots like banana and grasses, the leaf base has a sheath-like expansion that encircles the stem, called the...
bank.why: Monocot leaf bases sheathe the stem.

bank.q: A pair of leafy lateral outgrowths arising from the leaf base in many dicots.
bank.why: Stipules usually protect the developing buds.

bank.q: Leaves with stipules are called ___, as in Hibiscus and Ixora.
bank.why: With stipules = stipulate; without = exstipulate (Mangifera).

bank.q: Leaves without stipules, as in Mangifera, are...
bank.why: Ex- = without.

bank.q: In Ficus, the stipules are modified to...
bank.why: Ficus stipules enclose and protect the leaf bud.

bank.q: The stalk of a simple leaf is the ___, while that of a compound leaf is the ___.
bank.why: Simple → petiole; compound → rachis.

bank.q: Leaves without a stalk, as in Calotropis and Zinnia, are called...
bank.why: Sessile = no stalk; petiolate = with petiole.

bank.q: In which plant is the petiole wing-shaped?
bank.why: Citrus has a winged petiole.

bank.q: The green, thin, expanded part of the leaf involved in photosynthesis, respiration and transpiration.
bank.why: Its tip is the apex; its edge is the margin.

bank.q: The petiole extends throughout the lamina as a strong vein called the...
bank.why: Midrib → veins → veinlets form the framework.

bank.q: In grasses, the petiole is...
bank.why: The petiole is absent in grasses; in some palms it forms a rachis.

bank.q: Small outgrowths at the junction between the leaf base and the petiole in some monocots, like grasses.
bank.why: Ligules are found in grasses.

bank.q: The lamina of monocot leaves is isobilateral, meaning...
bank.a: The lower and upper sides are similar
d: It is folded in the bud
bank.why: Isobilateral = both sides alike.

bank.q: The pattern of arrangement of veins in the leaf blade.
bank.why: Two kinds: reticulate and parallel.

bank.q: Veins and veinlets form an anastomosing network. This is...
bank.why: Reticulate = network; typical of dicots.

bank.q: Reticulate venation is characteristic of ___ leaves, and parallel venation of ___ leaves.
bank.why: Dicot = net, monocot = parallel.

bank.q: Horizontal parallel venation is seen in...
bank.why: Horizontal: banana; longitudinal: bamboo, grasses, lilies.

bank.q: Which dicots show parallel venation (an exception)?
bank.why: Dicot exceptions with parallel venation.

bank.q: Which monocots show reticulate venation (an exception)?
bank.why: Monocot exceptions with net venation.

bank.q: A Mimosa pudica plant photosynthesizes normally but its leaves no longer fold at night or when touched. Which structure is most likely affected?
bank.why: The swollen pulvinus moves the leaf through turgor changes.

bank.q: In a Hibiscus mutant, developing buds are frequently damaged, though leaves photosynthesize normally. Which structures are most likely missing?
bank.why: Stipules protect the developing buds.

bank.q: A leaf's blade is green, but water and food cannot reach its edges. Which leaf structure is most likely damaged?
bank.why: The vein network serves as the transport channels of the lamina.

bank.term: Experiment: does the pulvinus move the leaf?
bank.q: A researcher wants to prove that the pulvinus causes Mimosa leaves to fold. What is the best design?
bank.a: Touch leaves on several plants after numbing or removing the pulvinus on some leaves while leaving others intact as controls, under the same light and temperature, then record which leaves fold
d: Touch one leaf and watch it fold
Water the plant and count the leaflets
Keep the plant in the dark for a week
bank.why: Only the pulvinus differs between treated and control leaves, so a difference in folding shows its role.

bank.q: A leaf with only a single lamina whose incisions do not touch the midrib.
bank.why: Simple leaf example: Hibiscus.

bank.q: A leaf whose lamina is divided into segments called leaflets or pinnae.
bank.why: Leaflets all connect to a common rachis.

bank.q: Unlike leaves, leaflets are devoid of ___ in their axils.
bank.why: No buds or stipules in leaflet axils.

bank.q: A compound leaf differs from a branch because it...
bank.a: Has no terminal or axillary buds and does not bear flowers or fruits
bank.why: Branches have nodes, buds, flowers and fruits; compound leaves do not.

bank.q: A compound leaf develops from a ___, while a branch develops from the ___.
bank.a: Node; axillary bud of a leaf
bank.why: Compound leaf: from a node. Branch: from an axillary bud.

bank.q: The two types of compound leaves are...
bank.why: Pinnate (feather) and palmate (hand).

bank.q: Leaflets arranged in two ranks on both sides of the rachis, like a bird's feather.
bank.why: Examples: neem, Moringa.

bank.q: Leaflets radiating from the tip of the rachis, like fingers on a palm.
bank.why: Palmate: unifoliate to multifoliate.

bank.q: Unipinnate leaflets that are paired and even-numbered; the rachis ends in a pair. This is...
bank.why: Paripinnate: unipinnate leaflets that are paired and even-numbered; the rachis ends in a pair. Example: Tamarindus.

bank.q: Which is an example of a paripinnate leaf?
bank.why: Paripinnate: Tamarindus.

bank.q: Unipinnate leaflets that are odd-numbered; the rachis ends in a single leaflet. This is...
bank.why: Imparipinnate: unipinnate leaflets that are odd-numbered; the rachis ends in a single leaflet. Example: Rose and neem.

bank.q: Which is an example of a imparipinnate leaf?
bank.why: Imparipinnate: Rose and neem.

bank.q: The primary rachis bears secondary axes (rachillae) bearing leaflets; pinnate twice. This is...
bank.why: Bipinnate: the primary rachis bears secondary axes (rachillae) bearing leaflets; pinnate twice. Example: Acacia and Mimosa pudica.

bank.q: Which is an example of a bipinnate leaf?
bank.why: Bipinnate: Acacia and Mimosa pudica.

bank.q: Primary rachis → secondary rachi → tertiary rachi bearing leaflets; pinnate thrice. This is...
bank.why: Tripinnate: primary rachis → secondary rachi → tertiary rachi bearing leaflets; pinnate thrice. Example: Moringa.

bank.q: Which is an example of a tripinnate leaf?
bank.why: Tripinnate: Moringa.

bank.q: Pinnately compound leaves pinnate more than thrice. This is...
bank.why: Decompound: pinnately compound leaves pinnate more than thrice. Example: Coriander.

bank.q: Which is an example of a decompound leaf?
bank.why: Decompound: Coriander.

bank.q: A palmately compound leaf with a single leaflet is...
bank.why: Unifoliate: a single leaflet (e.g. Citrus).

bank.q: Which is an example of a unifoliate leaf?
bank.why: Unifoliate: Citrus.

bank.q: A palmately compound leaf with two terminal leaflets is...
bank.why: Bifoliate: two terminal leaflets (e.g. Balanites, Bignonia).

bank.q: Which is an example of a bifoliate leaf?
bank.why: Bifoliate: Balanites, Bignonia.

bank.q: A palmately compound leaf with three terminal leaflets is...
bank.why: Trifoliate: three terminal leaflets (e.g. Trigonella, rubber).

bank.q: Which is an example of a trifoliate leaf?
bank.why: Trifoliate: Trigonella, rubber.

bank.q: A palmately compound leaf with four terminal leaflets is...
bank.why: Quadrifoliate: four terminal leaflets (e.g. Marsilea).

bank.q: Which is an example of a quadrifoliate leaf?
bank.why: Quadrifoliate: Marsilea.

bank.q: A palmately compound leaf with more than four terminal leaflets is...
bank.why: Multifoliate (digitate): more than four terminal leaflets (e.g. Bombax, tapioca).

bank.q: Which is an example of a multifoliate leaf?
bank.why: Multifoliate (digitate): Bombax, tapioca.

bank.q: How many kinds of palmately compound leaves are listed?
bank.why: Unifoliate, bifoliate, trifoliate, quadrifoliate, multifoliate.

bank.q: The 4 types of pinnately compound leaves are...
bank.why: Pinnate: uni, bi, tri, decompound.

bank.q: A student finds a leafy structure with several leaflets on a common axis but no buds anywhere on it and no flowers. What is it most likely?
bank.why: No terminal or axillary buds and no flowers → compound leaf.

bank.q: A Citrus leaf looks like a simple leaf, but it has a joint between the blade and the winged petiole. What is it?
bank.why: Citrus is unifoliate palmately compound.

bank.q: A student must decide whether a leafy axis is a branch or a compound leaf. What is the most reliable method?
bank.a: Check the axils of each leaflet and the tip of the axis for buds, look for nodes and internodes, and observe over time whether it ever bears flowers or fruits
d: Measure how long the axis is
Check whether the leaflets are green
bank.why: Buds, nodes and flowering are the features that separate branches from compound leaves.

bank.q: A lamina that is long and narrow (e.g. grasses) is...
bank.why: Linear: long and narrow.

bank.q: A lamina that is lance-shaped, long and tapering, broadest near the stalk (e.g. Nerium, bamboo) is...
bank.why: Lanceolate: lance-shaped, long and tapering, broadest near the stalk.

bank.q: A lamina that is lanceolate but broadest near the apex (e.g. Calamus) is...
bank.why: Oblanceolate: lanceolate but broadest near the apex.

bank.q: A lamina that is tapering at the ends, broad in the middle like an ellipse (e.g. guava, Vinca) is...
bank.why: Elliptical: tapering at the ends, broad in the middle like an ellipse.

bank.q: A lamina that is two or three times as long as broad, sides parallel, ends rounded (e.g. plantain, Ixora) is...
bank.why: Oblong: two or three times as long as broad, sides parallel, ends rounded.

bank.q: A lamina that is egg-shaped, slightly broader at the base (e.g. banyan) is...
bank.why: Ovate: egg-shaped, slightly broader at the base.

bank.q: A lamina that is inversely ovate, broader near the apex (e.g. Tectona) is...
bank.why: Obovate: inversely ovate, broader near the apex.

bank.q: A lamina that is more or less circular (e.g. lotus) is...
bank.why: Orbicular: more or less circular.

bank.q: A lamina that is heart-shaped (e.g. Thespesia) is...
bank.why: Cordate: heart-shaped.

bank.q: A lamina that is inversely heart-shaped (e.g. Oxalis leaflets) is...
bank.why: Obcordate: inversely heart-shaped.

bank.q: A lamina that is kidney-shaped with a broad shallow depression at the base (e.g. Centella) is...
bank.why: Reniform: kidney-shaped with a broad shallow depression at the base.

bank.q: A lamina that is arrowhead-shaped with two sharp straight lobes at the base (e.g. Sagittaria) is...
bank.why: Sagittate: arrowhead-shaped with two sharp straight lobes at the base.

bank.q: A lamina that is sickle-shaped, curved sideways (e.g. adult Eucalyptus leaves) is...
bank.why: Falcate: sickle-shaped, curved sideways.

bank.q: A lamina that is right and left halves not symmetrical (e.g. Begonia) is...
bank.why: Oblique: right and left halves not symmetrical.

bank.q: A lamina that is lyre-shaped, pinnatifid with a large terminal lobe (e.g. mustard) is...
bank.why: Lyrate: lyre-shaped, pinnatifid with a large terminal lobe.

bank.q: A lamina that is needle-shaped, long, narrow and cylindrical (e.g. Allium) is...
bank.why: Acicular: needle-shaped, long, narrow and cylindrical.

bank.q: A lamina that is strap-shaped (e.g. Vallisneria) is...
bank.why: Lorate: strap-shaped.

bank.q: In leaf shapes, the prefix "ob-" (obovate, obcordate, oblanceolate) means...
bank.a: The inverted form, broadest toward the apex
bank.why: Ob- = inverted: the broad part is near the tip.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is even and smooth (e.g. Mangifera) is...
bank.why: Entire margin: even and smooth.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is saw-like, with pointed teeth projecting upward (e.g. Balsam) is...
bank.why: Serrate margin: saw-like, with pointed teeth projecting upward.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is sharply pointed triangular teeth pointing outward (e.g. Hibiscus) is...
bank.why: Dentate margin: sharply pointed triangular teeth pointing outward.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is rounded, forward-pointing teeth (e.g. Bryophyllum) is...
bank.why: Crenate margin: rounded, forward-pointing teeth.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is wavy (e.g. Polyalthia) is...
bank.why: Undulate margin: wavy.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is provided with spines (e.g. pineapple, Aloe) is...
bank.why: Spiny margin: provided with spines.

bank.q: A leaf margin that is bearing fine cilia-like hairs (e.g. Cleome viscosa) is...
bank.why: Ciliate margin: bearing fine cilia-like hairs.

bank.q: Clefts that extend halfway to the midrib are called ___, while cuts that reach nearly to the midrib are called ___.
bank.why: Fid = halfway (castor, papaya); sect = nearly to the midrib (tapioca, rubber).

bank.q: A leaf apex that is sharply ending and abruptly pointed (e.g. Mangifera) is...
bank.why: Acute apex: sharply ending and abruptly pointed.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is narrowing to a long slender tail (e.g. Ficus religiosa) is...
bank.why: Acuminate apex: narrowing to a long slender tail.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is blunt or rounded (e.g. banyan) is...
bank.why: Obtuse apex: blunt or rounded.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is ending in a long, rigid, spiny point (e.g. pineapple) is...
bank.why: Cuspidate apex: ending in a long, rigid, spiny point.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is rounded, ending abruptly in a short sharp point (e.g. Crotalaria) is...
bank.why: Mucronate apex: rounded, ending abruptly in a short sharp point.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is bluntly rounded with a shallow central notch (e.g. Calophyllum) is...
bank.why: Retuse apex: bluntly rounded with a shallow central notch.

bank.q: A leaf apex that is with a deep notch at the tip (e.g. Bauhinia) is...
bank.why: Emarginate apex: with a deep notch at the tip.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is smooth and shiny is...
bank.why: Glabrous: smooth and shiny.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is covered with short, soft hairs is...
bank.why: Pubescent: covered with short, soft hairs.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is thickly covered with soft, long hairs is...
bank.why: Villous: thickly covered with soft, long hairs.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is covered with stiff hairs is...
bank.why: Hispid: covered with stiff hairs.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is rough with short, stiff hairs is...
bank.why: Scabrous: rough with short, stiff hairs.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is completely covered with matted hairs is...
bank.why: Tomentose: completely covered with matted hairs.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is with translucent oil spots seen against the light is...
bank.why: Gland dotted: with translucent oil spots seen against the light.

bank.q: A leaf surface that is with silky hairs and a silken sheen is...
bank.why: Sericeous: with silky hairs and a silken sheen.

bank.q: When a Citrus leaf is held against the light, translucent spots appear. Each spot is a place where...
bank.why: Gland-dotted surface: each spot stores oil.

bank.q: Two mango-like leaves differ only at the tip: leaf A ends in a long slender tail, leaf B ends sharply without a tail. Their apices are...
bank.why: Acuminate = long tail (Ficus religiosa); acute = sharp, abrupt point.

bank.q: Two Hibiscus varieties grow in a dry area; the pubescent one loses less water than the glabrous one. Which explains this?
bank.a: Its hairs trap a layer of moist air and reduce water loss
d: Its hairs absorb water from the soil
bank.why: Trichomes (hairs) can trap moist air and reduce water loss.

bank.q: The pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem and branches.
bank.why: Phyllotaxy = leaf arrangement on the stem.

bank.q: The main purpose of phyllotaxy is to...
bank.a: Provide sufficient light to the leaves
bank.why: Arranging leaves reduces shading.

bank.q: The form and arrangement of foliage leaves in buds.
bank.why: Prefoliation = leaves in buds.

bank.q: The form in which young leaves are folded or rolled on themselves in the bud.
bank.why: Ptyxis = folding of each young leaf.

bank.q: The arrangement of leaves within a bud.
bank.why: Vernation (not venation!) = leaves within the bud.

bank.q: Leaves arranged in a cluster on a very short, stumpy stem on top of the root, as in radish.
bank.why: Radical = at the root top; cauline = on a stem with internodes.

bank.q: The three main types of cauline phyllotaxy are...
bank.why: Cauline: alternate, opposite, whorled.

bank.q: Leaves on alternate nodes, with only a single leaf on each node.
bank.why: Alternate = 1 per node.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged in two vertical rows on the two sides of the stem (Annona, grasses).
bank.why: Di = two rows.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged in three rows, as in Cyperus.
bank.why: Tri = three rows.

bank.q: Alternate leaves arranged spirally around the stem, as in Hibiscus.
bank.why: Spiral alternate: Hibiscus.

bank.q: A pair of leaves arranged oppositely on each node.
bank.why: Opposite = 2 per node.

bank.q: Opposite phyllotaxy in which adjacent pairs are at right angles to each other (Ixora, Calotropis).
bank.why: Decussate = crossed at right angles.

bank.q: Opposite phyllotaxy in which adjacent pairs are exactly one above the other in the same plane (Quisqualis).
bank.why: Superposed = stacked directly above.

bank.q: Three or more leaves arising from each node in a circle around the stem (Nerium, Alstonia).
bank.why: Whorled = 3+ per node.

bank.q: Leaves are modified in different ways for...
bank.why: Tendrils, hooks, spines, scales, pitchers, phyllodes.

bank.q: Long, spirally coiled, spring-like leaves that help weak-stemmed plants climb.
bank.why: Leaf tendrils are sensitive to contact (Pisum, Gloriosa, Lathyrus).

bank.q: In Pisum, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Pisum: tendrils are modified terminal leaflets.

bank.q: In Gloriosa, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Gloriosa: tendrils are modified leaf tips.

bank.q: In Lathyrus (sweet pea), leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Lathyrus (sweet pea): tendrils are entire leaves.

bank.q: In Clematis, leaf tendrils are...
bank.why: Clematis: tendrils are modified rachillae.

bank.q: Hook-like modifications of the terminal leaflets for clinging, as in Bignonia unguis-cati.
bank.why: Three terminal leaflets become cat-claw hooks.

bank.q: Sharply pointed leaf modifications characteristic of xerophytes like cacti.
bank.why: Spines: defense, protection and control of transpiration.

bank.q: In Ananas (pineapple) and Agave, leaf spines are modified...
bank.why: Opuntia: minute leaves of axillary buds; Ananas/Agave: leaf margins.

bank.q: Thin, stalkless, membranous leaves that protect the axillary buds in their axils.
bank.why: In onion they are fleshy, storing water, mucilage and food.

bank.q: A flask-shaped modification of the leaf lamina for trapping insects (Nepenthes, Sarracenia).
bank.why: Insectivorous plants trap insects in pitchers.

bank.q: In Nepenthes, the lid covering the mouth of the pitcher is the...
bank.why: The operculum is a modified part of the leaf tip.

bank.q: In Nepenthes, which part of the leaf is modified into the pitcher?
bank.why: The lamina becomes the pitcher; the petiole is flat and tendril-like.

bank.q: A flat, leaf-like, photosynthetic modification of the petiole or rachis.
bank.why: Phyllodes are xerophytic adaptations (Acacia, Parkinsonia).

bank.q: A phyllode is a ___ modification, while a phylloclade is a ___ modification.
bank.why: Phyllode = petiole/rachis; phylloclade = stem.

bank.q: Which describes a phyllode, not a phylloclade?
bank.a: Unbranched, no nodes and internodes, never succulent
bank.why: Phyllodes lack nodes; phylloclades have them and are succulent.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the functions of leaves listed?
d: Help in pollination by attractive coloration
bank.why: Anchorage is a root function.

bank.q: In a plant mutant, every leaf grows from the same side of the stem and the lower leaves are heavily shaded. What is most likely affected?
bank.why: Phyllotaxy arranges leaves to provide sufficient light.

bank.q: A Nepenthes plant's pitchers trap insects, but the insects are never digested and the plant lacks nitrogen. What is most likely not working?
bank.a: Enzyme secretion by the pitcher wall
bank.why: Insects are digested by enzymes secreted by the pitcher wall.

bank.q: Insects slip into a pitcher but many escape before being digested. Which part is most likely not closing?
bank.why: The operculum closes the mouth to prevent escape.

bank.q: An Australian Acacia loses its leaflets early, yet keeps photosynthesizing with flat structures, saving water. What are they?
bank.why: In Acacia, the rachis flattens into a leaf-like phyllode.

bank.q: A pea plant's leaves photosynthesize normally, but the plant cannot climb its support. Which leaf part is most likely affected?
bank.why: In Pisum, the terminal leaflets become tendrils.

bank.q: Spines are removed from a group of cacti in a dry field. Compared with untouched cacti, what would you most likely observe?
bank.a: More grazing damage and more water loss
d: Faster photosynthesis and no other change
bank.why: Leaf spines defend, protect and control transpiration.

bank.q: A researcher wants to test whether leaf arrangement affects how much light lower leaves receive. Which design is most appropriate?
bank.a: Grow plants of one species with the same height and leaf number, measure light at their lower leaves with a light meter under one lamp, and compare with plants whose leaves were repositioned to overlap, repeating with several plants
d: Compare one tall tree with one short herb
Count the leaves on several different species
Move the plants to the shade and measure their height
bank.why: Same species, size and light source keep everything constant except the arrangement; repeats make the result reliable.
bank.hint: Same plant, change only the arrangement.

bank.term: Leaves keep growing but stem doesn't
